newsitem.title: EGYPT: U.S. envoy criticises Egypt policy on conference.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy criticises Egypt policy on conference.

text.p: A U.S. envoy implicitly criticised Egypt on Tuesday for its view that holding a Middle East economic conference in November depends on progress towards peace.

"There is no fixed timetable for making progress so there is no linkage between making progress and holding the conference," U.S. special Middle East coordinator Dennis Ross said after talks with Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa.

Moussa and Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak have made the link in repeated statements this month and Moussa said again on Tuesday that the new Israeli government had not yet done enough to advance talks with Syria and the Palestinians.

"We believe that recent statements from Israel indicate a lack of interest in the peace process and help to poison the atmosphere more and more at a time when we are trying to put blood back into the veins of the process," he told reporters.
Both Ross and Moussa said they were still working on preparations for the conference and Ross noted that Mubarak has said he is keen that the conference take place on time.

But Moussa added: "We are talking about holding the economic conference and we call on Israel to take steps and measures to put the peace process back on track. Israel's response to that so far has not been acceptable to our side."

In an interview published in Wednesday's Egyptian government newspapers, Mubarak repeated his view that the conference, designed to integrate Israel into the regional economy, would be pointless unless the atmosphere was right.
"We still have time," he added. "There must be a move to change the current atmosphere and provide the trust now lost because of the hardline statements coming out of Israel."
"So we are asking America and Israel to work in the time that's left until the date for the conference to provide a chance for it to succeed," Mubarak added.

Ross said he would not be visiting Syria during his current tour but U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher would meet Syrian Foreign Minister Farouq al-Shara next week during the U.N. General Assembly session in New York.
He will go to Gaza to see Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and discuss both Israeli-Palestinian talks and the results of a recent aid donors meeting.
Ross will meet Mubarak on Wednesday at his summer holiday home near the Mediterranean city of Alexandria.
Both Ross and Moussa shed no new light on U.S. proposals for persuading Israel and Syria to resume direct peace talks.
Moussa said: "No proposals have been announced but there have been reports of activities and contacts. The U.S. role must be activated because much depends on that."
"The situation, it seems today, is very serious and is leading to a feeling of frustration," he added.
